title: Why just-in-time sourcing doesn't kill the price argument
deck: The sharpest bear case against the framework isn't about adoption — it's about inventory. If banks source XRP three seconds before each transaction and dump it immediately after, does the price argument collapse? The answer reveals something the series left implicit.

title: The derivatives market doesn't break the model. It completes it.
deck: A reader challenged whether using spot-only volume understates XRP's settlement capacity. The answer is counterintuitive: spot-only is the correct input for settlement analysis, and a deep derivatives market is a precondition for the thesis — not a competing narrative.

title: Batch transactions on the XRPL: what they mean for the settlement thesis.
deck: The series has not addressed batch transactions on the XRPL. It should. A native protocol feature that bundles multiple atomic payments through XRP changes the liquidity demand picture — and its near-miss with a critical bug tells us something important about where the protocol is in its maturity curve.

title: Two price drivers the model doesn't capture — and why one matters more than the other.
deck: A reader argued the framework misses FASB ASC 350-60 supply depletion and HFT velocity recycling. Both deserve serious engagement. One identifies a genuine gap in the model. The other conflates two distinct kinds of velocity — and the distinction reveals something important about how the market is actually structured.

title: The price that doesn't collapse on itself.
deck: There is a calculable equilibrium band at every stage of adoption — wide enough that liquidity providers are rational to hold inventory, narrow enough that the asset isn't priced so far ahead of utility that a delay becomes a collapse. The series never formalized it. This note does.

title: The transaction that cannot be made smaller.
deck: Prisma and transaction-splitting change how ODL executes. They do not change what institutional settlement requires. There is a class of cross-border transactions that cannot be netted, layered, or split below a threshold — and that threshold is where the framework's price logic lives.

title: The workaround that isn't.
deck: AMMs, PayFi, ETF hoarding, and CBDC closed loops. Four objections from the current competitive landscape that target the framework's mechanical assumptions — not its adoption conditions. Each is answered on its own terms. One partial concession is made.

title: The network finds the liquidity. Until it can't.
deck: XRPL's pathfinding and dynamic liquidity assembly change the picture at smaller ticket sizes. A serious practitioner pushed on whether the static depth assumption overstates the requirement. He's right — up to a point. This note finds that point.

title: This is not Ripple's preferred arrangement.
deck: The sharpest empirical objection to this framework is that XRP is largely invisible in Ripple's own institutional stack. The objection is accurate. What it misreads is why — and what the legal record shows Ripple has been trying to do about it from the moment it legally could.

title: The pathfinding threshold — a framework for the most important unanswered question.
deck: ISO Ledger audited the full series and closed with one open question: at what specific adoption threshold does XRPL's dynamic liquidity assembly stop compensating for insufficient static depth? They called it the most important number in the framework. Here is a framework for thinking about the answer.

title: A live look at the system, and where we go from here.
deck: The series has modeled what the system requires. This note looks at what the system actually is — right now, with real on-chain data. Only 5–8 billion XRP is consistently available for settlement execution today. Here is what that means, and what changes as price appreciates through a series of economic activation thresholds.

title: The speculative decoupling — what the ATH proves about the framework.
deck: XRP's all-time high of $3.65 on July 18, 2025 produced the largest market cap in the asset's history. The framework's own formula shows it also produced one of the weakest peak ticket capacities of recent years. This field note runs the confirmed numbers — and explains what the gap reveals about what kind of event the ATH actually was.

title: The leg that cannot move first.
subtitle: The property that cannot be separated.
deck: Prisma can split PvP flows. It cannot split DvP. The atomicity that eliminates principal risk is the same property that prohibits leg-decoupled partial execution. Most settlement flows use conditional escrow and are priced by MV=PQ. A narrower class cannot be split — and for those transactions, peak ticket depth governs everything.

title: The source list — they weren't writing about XRP.
deck: Every primary document behind the series. BIS, IMF, NY Fed, TBAC, SEC, DTCC, XRPL. None of them mention XRP. All of them describe the problems XRP is built to solve. Read them yourself.

title: The room gets built.
deck: Four DTCC and SEC announcements in fourteen days. The ledger layer named. The data layer named. The working group named — including Ripple Prime, explicitly, in the press release. The timeline named. The one thing DTCC has not named is the cross-border value settlement asset. That chair is still empty. That chair is what this series has always been about.

title: The $13 trillion question.
deck: The SEC Chair named the problem. The private networks cannot solve it. The stablecoin float is a fraction of what is needed — and it is not even fully available for this one use case. Here is the arithmetic, and why every escape route dead-ends at the same wall.
